CausalChain: HepG2 cells inherently possess a fetal, hepatoblastoma-like profile with low CYP enzyme expression -> 2D culture conditions fail to support mature hepatocyte phenotypes -> 3D spheroid cultures have been shown to restore aspects of liver-specific functions through enhanced cell-cell interactions and altered signaling -> The aberrant Wnt/β-catenin pathway in HepG2 cells contributes to their less differentiated state -> Modulating Wnt/β-catenin signaling in a 3D culture environment can drive epigenetic changes and reactivate phase I enzyme expression -> Therefore, shifting HepG2 cells to a 3D environment with targeted pathway modulation may promote a more adult hepatocyte-like metabolic profile.
Hypothesis: Imposing 3D spheroid culture conditions combined with targeted modulation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway will reprogram HepG2 cells to upregulate phase I drug-metabolizing enzymes, thereby transforming their phenotype from a hepatoblastoma-like state to a more mature hepatocyte-like state suitable for accurate xenobiotic metabolism studies.
Abstract: HepG2 cells, while widely used as an in vitro model of liver function, display a unique molecular profile that more closely resembles hepatoblastoma than mature hepatocytes, particularly with respect to their low expression of key phase I metabolic enzymes. Recent evidence suggests that culture dimensionality strongly influences cellular phenotype and gene expression. In this review, we propose that transitioning HepG2 cells from traditional 2D monolayer cultures to three‐dimensional (3D) spheroid systems – in combination with targeted modulation of signaling pathways such as Wnt/β‐catenin – may induce epigenetic reprogramming toward a more differentiated, hepatocyte‐like state. This reprogramming is hypothesized to enhance the expression and activity of drug‐metabolizing cytochromes, thereby improving the predictive validity of HepG2s in drug metabolism and toxicity studies. Our hypothesis lays the groundwork for experimental validation, potentially bridging the gap between hepatoblastoma models and true hepatocyte function in vitro.
